segments.text: Today I am building the brain function for my personal AI assistant Borax, and the first question is what should the system remember?
Most people make this mistake: they put every responsibility into one giant file, and then the assistant becomes impossible to maintain.
The better approach is a clear three-step system. First understand the request, second select the right capability, and third verify the result.
Here is the surprising part. A useful AI assistant does not need to be the largest model; it needs reliable memory, tools, and recovery.
That single design decision can save hours of debugging and lets every component improve without breaking the entire application.
If you are creating your own Jarvis-style assistant, stop chasing features for a moment and build one dependable workflow from beginning to end.
When that workflow can accept an instruction, take an action, report progress, and recover from failure, you have created the foundation.
The secret is not more code. The secret is separating the brain, memory, tools, permissions, and user interface into modules.
This makes the assistant faster on a normal laptop and gives you a clear place to fix a problem when something goes wrong.
Before you call the project finished, test the complete experience like a real user: start the server, upload a file, and verify the output.
That final verification is what turns an interesting demo into a product people can trust.
